chapter: First bass jobs in California, Chicago and the move to New York
title: Chicago bandleaders and clubs after Les Wilcox
summary: He lists the Chicago leaders he worked for, starting with Les Wilcox, and the Club De Luxe.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: So Roy said (unintelligible). I went up to the bandstand, took the base. First note, Art got up, he didn't have to look up, he knew who it was. So I stayed around there, and I worked with a wonderful musician, a bandleader, four pieces combo -- Les Wilcox. He could write and arrange individual parts. He could write music like you would write a letter, in long-hand. No score. This is the first time I had ever seen anything like that. He liked me. And they didn't have a bass player. So I'd go over there and sit, play with them every night. Didn't have a dime. Waitress would feed me one night, bartender would feed me another, band would feed me one night. They would take turns.
So then I worked with bands such as Tony Fambrough, Danny Williams, Johnny Long, black Johnny Long, not the white Johnny Long. He was a trumpet player and a cosmetologist.
Yeah. Tiny Parham, Erskine Tate, Charles Elgar. I'm sure there's more. John Letmann -- that's where Ray Nance was working the floor show when he joined Duke. dope.
Joe Hughes' Club De Luxe. 63rd and South Park. And Johnny Letmann had the band. So Roy came in town.
